title: Sky figures of South Asia
unit: One record is one figure, as one culture draws it, from one source.
method: A figure is a stronger claim than a name. A name says a language calls these stars something; a figure says it joins them into a shape, and drawing a line between two stars asserts that the source saw one there. So a figure is recorded as PARTS — the roles the source names and the stars it gives them — and never as a polyline invented to make a picture. Where a source names a role without saying which stars fill it, the part is recorded with an empty star list and `attested: false`, because the role is real even when the assignment is not. Lines are derived at export time from parts, never authored here.

figures.scene: The cot doubles as the bier that carries a corpse to the grave. After the burial one side of the frame is broken and the bed is left at the burial ground; the watchman on the threshing floor, waking cold before dawn, sees the broken frame in the north and the mourners walking away from it.

parts.role: the broken frame of the bier
parts.note: Hoffmann's four stars, which the entry contrasts with the same four read as Saptarṣi — 'an entirely different mood'.

parts.role: the mourners walking away from the grave
parts.note: Alioth and Mizar, both named in the source.

figures.citation: Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Mundarica, vol. VII, s.v. ipil, cols. 1919-1925
figures.notes: Alkaid is left unassigned because the source assigns it nothing. The first element of the name is printed topagara/topogara in the two scans and could not be checked; only 'the bier stars' is secure.

figures.name_meaning: a cot, its shape distorted because a thief pulled at one of its legs
figures.scene: Three thieves at a cot. The four legs were of gold, silver, copper and iron, and a thief pulled the golden one — which is why the bowl is not a true rectangle. Individual villages substitute a local cast for the thieves: the village elder, the chief and the sheriff, or the revenue collector in place of the elder.

parts.role: the four legs of the cot
parts.note: The four bowl stars. Which of them is the golden leg that was pulled is not stated; the survey gives the reasoning — the bowl is out of square — but names no star.

parts.role: the three thieves
parts.note: The three handle stars. The Kolams of the same survey make them a Kolam, a Gond and a Pardhan; the Bhils make them the men who come to the village to take things from it.

parts.role: the middle thief's child, or her pregnancy
parts.note: Alcor beside Mizar. Most villages see it and call the middle thief a pregnant woman.

figures.citation: Shreya Shetye, Ganesh Halkare and Aniket Sule, 'Bhil, Pawra and Kokna astronomy', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage (2023)
figures.notes: The paper prints no Bhili word for the cot itself, so the figure is recorded without a vernacular name — the precedent is the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entry in tribal.json. The survey covered 210 people in 17 meetings across the Bhil, Mavchi Bhil, Vasave Bhil, Pawra and Kokna communities of north-western Maharashtra.

figures.name_meaning: a Mahua tree (Madhuca longifolia), whose flowers are fermented to make liquor
figures.scene: A Mahua tree with two women gathering its flowers beneath it — an old lady and a young one — and the faint stars around them are the flowers themselves. The tree is named for the crop: Mahua flowers are collected in March and April.

parts.role: the Mahua tree
parts.note: The four stars of Crux.

parts.role: the old lady and the young one, gathering flowers
parts.note: Named in the source as α and β Centauri — Murta and Kadma, which the database carries as names in their own right.

parts.role: the flowers of the Mahua
parts.note: Irup pokke, 'the flowers of the Mahua' — the small stars around the tree. The source says faint stars, and names none of them.

figures.citation: M.N. Vahia, Ganesh Halkare, Kishore Menon and Harini Calamur, 'The astronomy of two Indian tribes: the Banjaras and the Kolams', Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage 17(1) (2014)
figures.notes: Eight of ten villages. The figure spans two IAU constellations, which is why it cannot be expressed as a constellation and has to be expressed as a figure. It also closes an identification tribal.json had to leave open: Gondi Irukna Mara, recorded there as `unidentified`, is transparently the same word.

figures.name_meaning: Dingdi's cloth-stretching, puan being a cloth
figures.scene: A scene indoors: a girl named Dingdi at her loom, with the cloth she is weaving pinned to the wall at two points that are themselves stars. A named character, an action, and two stars doing duty as nails in a wall.

parts.role: Dingdi at the apex of the triangle
parts.note: Capella, named in the source.

parts.role: the two points where the cloth is pinned to the wall
parts.note: Lorrain gives an isosceles triangle in Auriga with Capella at its apex, and does not say which two stars are the base. They are not assigned here.

figures.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Dingdi-puan-tah
figures.notes: The best-drawn figure in the database. Most sky-figures here are a single object — a cot, a plough, a deer; this one is a domestic scene, and its only counterpart is the Kolam Mahua tree.

figures.scene: Joining all seven stars gives a karacūli with a handle — independently the same idea as the English Dipper.

parts.role: the ladle, joined from all seven
parts.note: Praharaj's note says joining the seven yields the shape, which assigns the whole set and no part of it separately.

figures.citation: G. C. Praharaj, Purnnachandra Ordia Bhashakosha: a lexicon of the Oriya language, Cuttack: Utkal Sahitya Press, 1931-40, s.v. Sātabhāiyā
figures.notes: Recorded because the source states the joining explicitly, which most do not. The shape it yields is the same as the standard figure — a figure agreeing with the received one is still a figure, and saying so is worth more than leaving it out.

figures.name_meaning: the Gangetic river-dolphin, the whole sky coiled into one animal
figures.scene: The entire host of lights described as one creature, 'for fixing the mind in yoga on Bhagavān Vāsudeva' (5.23.4). It hangs head-down, its body coiled clockwise, with Dhruva at the tip of its tail so that the beast turns about the pole. The nakshatras of the sun's northern path lie along its right side and those of the southern path along its left, the same number on each; Ajavīthī the goat-road is its back and the Milky Way its belly. The planets ride it too — the Sun at its chest, the Moon in its mind, Mars at its mouth, Jupiter on its hump, Venus at its navel, Saturn at its genitals, Mercury as its breaths, Rāhu at its throat, the comets in all its limbs — and every remaining star is a hair of its body. The chapter closes by prescribing it as an evening litany: at each sandhyā, restrained and silent, gazing on it, 'homage to the abode of the lights' (5.23.8).

parts.role: Dhruva, at the tip of the tail (pucchāgra)
parts.note: Polaris, in the received tradition; the older textual layer may intend Thuban (α Draconis) — see the Dhruva entry in the database.

parts.role: Prajāpati, Agni, Indra and Dharma, on the tail (lāṅgūla)
parts.note: Unidentified circumpolar stars along Draco / Ursa Minor. No Purāṇa says which four, and no star is chosen for them here.

parts.role: Dhātā and Vidhātā, at the root of the tail (puccha-mūla)
parts.note: Unidentified; circumpolar.

parts.role: the Seven Sages, at the waist (kaṭi)
parts.note: Saptarṣayaḥ — the Big Dipper, certain by universal tradition, though the Purāṇa itself never says which stars the Sages are.

parts.role: Ajavīthī, the goat-road, along the back (pṛṣṭha)
parts.note: A star-road, not a star: Mūla and the two Aṣāḍhās per Brahmāṇḍa/Matsya 124.53, but Matsya 124.58 instead gives Hasta, Citrā and Svātī — the vīthī texts contradict one another, so no stars are claimed.

parts.role: Ākāśagaṅgā, the sky-Ganges, at the belly (udara)
parts.note: The Milky Way — a band, not stars. The app draws it as its own layer.

parts.role: Punarvasu, the right hip (śroṇī)
parts.note: Castor and Pollux.

parts.role: Puṣya, the left hip (śroṇī)
parts.note: γ and δ Cancri. The database glosses Puṣya as γ/δ/θ Cancri; θ, at magnitude 5.3, is not in the vendored chart and is left out rather than replaced.

parts.role: Ārdrā, the right hind foot (paścima pāda)
parts.note: Betelgeuse. Sanyal's printed translation puts the hind feet on the nostrils — see the database's caveats; the text's own order is followed here.

parts.role: Āśleṣā, the left hind foot (paścima pāda)
parts.note: ε, δ and σ Hydrae — the head of Hydra.

parts.role: Abhijit, the right nostril (nāsikā)
parts.note: Vega — the 28th nakshatra, standing in the figure although it had already fallen out of the working roster (Mahābhārata 3.230).

parts.role: Uttarāṣāḍhā, the left nostril (nāsikā)
parts.note: σ and ζ Sagittarii.

parts.role: Śravaṇa, the right eye (locana)
parts.note: Altair.

parts.role: Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the left eye (locana)
parts.note: δ and ε Sagittarii.

parts.role: Dhaniṣṭhā, the right ear (karṇa)
parts.note: β and α Delphini, of the Dhaniṣṭhā diamond.

parts.role: Mūla, the left ear (karṇa)
parts.note: λ and υ Scorpii — the stinger.

parts.role: the eight southern-path nakshatras beginning with Maghā, as the ribs of the left side (vāma-pārśva-vaṅkri)
parts.note: Maghā through Anurādhā, one junction star each: Regulus, Zosma, Denebola, Gienah, Spica, Arcturus, ι Librae, Dschubba. The text says 'the eight beginning with Maghā'; the terminus is supplied by commentators and confirmed by counting. Viśākhā is carried at ι Librae, the database's reading — the Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna's two-star horn shape would put it at α/β Librae instead.

parts.role: the eight northern-path nakshatras beginning with Mṛgaśīrṣa, counted backwards, as the ribs of the right side (dakṣiṇa-pārśva-vaṅkri)
parts.note: Mṛgaśiras back through Pūrvabhādrapadā (prātilomyena), one junction star each: Meissa, Aldebaran, Alcyone, 35 Arietis, Sheratan, ζ Piscium, Algenib, Markab. The terminus is inferred, and confirmed by counting.

parts.role: Śatabhiṣā, the right shoulder (skandha)
parts.note: λ Aquarii — Sāmanta's re-observation, the same star the nakshatra layer marks.

parts.role: Jyeṣṭhā, the left shoulder (skandha)
parts.note: Antares.

parts.role: Agasti, the upper jaw (uttarā-hanu)
parts.note: Canopus — certain by universal tradition, not asserted by the text.

parts.role: Yama, the lower jaw (adharā-hanu)
parts.note: Unidentified. If Agasti is Canopus the jaw should hang in the far southern sky, and no source names its star.

figures.citation: Bhāgavata-purāṇa 5.23.5-7; the frame at 5.23.4 and the litany at 5.23.8
figures.notes: The one figure the Sanskrit tradition itself draws star by star. The older recension (Viṣṇu-purāṇa 2.12.29-34, with Matsya, Vāyu and Brahmāṇḍa parallels) is a compact circumpolar beast whose limbs are deities — only Dhruva of its stars is identifiable, and Matsya 125.3-7 arrays it on fourteen stars it does not name — so it is the Bhāgavata's expansion, which seats the named nakshatras on the body, that can be drawn at all. The star for each single-star nakshatra is its junction star (yogatārā) as the database identifies it — an identification of the nakshatra, not an assignment made by the Purāṇa. The planets, Nārāyaṇa at the heart, and the star-field as body-hair are in the scene, not the parts: they are not fixed stars, and a HIP number would be a false claim.

figures.name_meaning: Rohiṇī's cart — the V of the Hyades as a wain
figures.scene: The one nakshatra whose shape the census states with a count: the Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna gives Rohiṇī five stars 'shaped like a wagon', with venison for its food and Prajāpati for its deity. The omen literature then watches the cart as a thing that can be damaged: if Saturn, Mars or a comet splits it — śakaṭa-bheda, driving through the gap of the V — the world goes hungry, and the Skanda-purāṇa closes the story with an etiology: since then, Saturn does not split Rohiṇī's Cart.

parts.role: the cart, the five stars of Rohiṇī
parts.note: Aldebaran with θ², ε, δ and γ Tauri — the V of the Hyades. The census counts five; the database's identification adds θ¹, a fraction of a degree from θ², which the chart carries as a separate star and this record leaves to the note.

figures.citation: Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna, nakṣatra-vaṃśa (Divyāvadāna 33, p. 46-47: pañcatāraṃ śakaṭākāra-saṃsthānam); Bṛhat-saṃhitā 46.13-14 (śakaṭa-bheda) and 24.28-30
figures.notes: Like the Odia ladle, a whole-set claim: the sources give the shape and the count, never a vertex-by-vertex assignment, so the record is one part and the lines drawn are the received figure's own joins through the V.

figures.name_meaning: the deer — Prajāpati pierced, with the doe, the three-jointed arrow and the hunter
figures.scene: Prajāpati desired his own daughter — the sky, some say; Uṣas, say others. He became a stag and approached her as a doe. The gods assembled their most terrible forms into one being, who aimed and pierced him; pierced, he flew upward — 'and him they call the Deer'. The piercer is the Deer-piercer, of that very name; the doe is Rohiṇī; the three-jointed arrow is still the arrow. A hunt frozen across three constellations, told as the reason the sky looks the way it does.

parts.role: the deer's head (Mṛgaśiras)
parts.note: Meissa, λ Orionis — the nakshatra of the head. The received head adds φ¹ and φ² Orionis, which the vendored chart does not carry.

parts.role: the three-jointed arrow (iṣus trikāṇḍā), lodged in the deer
parts.note: The Belt — Mintaka, Alnilam, Alnitak — joined as the received figure joins it.

parts.role: the deer-piercer (Mṛgavyādha)
parts.note: Sirius, on the dominant identification — the Sūrya-siddhānta's catalogue places Mṛgavyādha at the twentieth degree of Gemini, forty south, which fits; Sāmanta re-observed it. The database keeps the identification 'disputed' and so does this record.

parts.role: the doe, Rohiṇī
parts.note: Aldebaran — the same star the cart figure claims, wearing a different story.

figures.notes: The oldest drawn figure in the record: a Brāhmaṇa-period tableau that only works across constellation boundaries — deer in Orion, hunter in Canis Major, doe in Taurus — which is exactly what the spans field exists to declare. The Brāhmaṇa names the cast; the star identifications are the received ones the database carries, with Mṛgavyādha's marked disputed there and here.

figures.name_meaning: the Seven Sages, with Arundhatī keeping close to Vasiṣṭha
figures.scene: The Ṛgveda already asks after these stars: 'those ṛkṣāḥ set on high, seen at night — where do they go by day?', and the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa remembers that the Seven Sages were formerly called the Bears. Varāhamihira names the seven in order, rising in the north-east — Marīci, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu — 'and there the virtuous Arundhatī keeps close to sage Vasiṣṭha'. The pair is the tradition's eyesight test and its wedding blessing at once: the bride is shown Arundhatī with the Seven, and the physicians say that one who cannot see her will not live the year.

parts.role: the seven sages, named in order
parts.note: In the Bṛhat-saṃhitā's order from the east: Marīci (Alkaid), Vasiṣṭha (Mizar), Aṅgiras (Alioth), Atri (Megrez), Pulastya (Phecda), Pulaha (Merak), Kratu (Dubhe). The text gives the names and the order; star-by-star seating is the received identification the database carries.

parts.role: Arundhatī, keeping close to sage Vasiṣṭha
parts.note: Alcor, beside Mizar — the one per-star claim the text itself makes, and the pair every source watches.

figures.citation: Bṛhat-saṃhitā 13.5-6; the ṛkṣa lineage at Ṛgveda 1.24.10 and Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.4; the wedding rite at Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra 1.7.22
figures.notes: The same seven stars the Mundari bier and the Bhili cot read entirely otherwise — which is the reason the figures layer exists. The seven are one part, not seven: the text assigns the set and the order, not star to name, and the record does not claim more than the text does.

figures.name_meaning: the seven Kṛttikās, each with her own name
figures.scene: The yajus names the seven one by one: Ambā, Dulā, Nitatnī, Abhrayantī, Meghayantī, Varṣayantī, Cupuṇīkā — and the last four are rain-names, she-who-brings-the-clouds, she-who-makes-them-rain. The Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa remembers who they are: the Kṛttikās were the wives of the Bears, the Seven Sages who stand in the north — which is why the two sets of seven face each other across the sky.

parts.role: the seven Kṛttikās, named one by one
parts.note: Six of the seven stand in the vendored chart: Alcyone, Atlas, Electra, Maia, Merope, Taygeta. Pleione, the seventh bright sister, is below its field limit and left to this note. Like the Saptarṣi, the text assigns the set and the names, never star to name.

figures.citation: Taittirīya-brāhmaṇa 3.1.4.1; the wives of the Bears at Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.4
figures.notes: The one nakshatra whose constituent stars the Veda names individually. The names are the record's; which sister is which star nobody says, so the figure is one part of six placed stars, and the seventh is a gap the chart made, not the text.

figures.name_meaning: Viṣṇu of the three strides; three star-pairs as his three footprints
figures.scene: Viṣṇu, as the dwarf who grew, crossed the worlds in three strides — and the catalogue reads the three faint star-pairs strung along the Bear's southern paws as the three footprints (pādān) he left on the sky. The same three pairs are the Arabic tradition's leaps of the gazelle; Nityānanda saw strides where the desert saw springs.

parts.role: the first footprint (yugmaka)
parts.note: ι and κ UMa — the pair the catalogue counts first.

parts.role: the second footprint (yugmaka)
parts.note: λ and μ UMa.

parts.role: the third footprint (yugmaka)
parts.note: ν and ξ UMa.

figures.citation: Sarvasiddhāntarāja, saṃkrāntyādi 27 and Nityānanda's own note (ed. Pai & Shylaja, JApA 42:113 (2021), n. 36); discussed in Shylaja & Pai, JAHH 22(2) (2019), 296–298
figures.notes: The one figure of the astrolabe-era catalogues: Pai & Shylaja call it hitherto unknown. Each footprint is a two-star pair the text itself calls a yugmaka and jointly pādān, 'the feet' — the pairing is the source's own, so all three lines are attested, and no line joins the footprints to each other: three prints, not a path. Shylaja links the figure to the Trivikrama of the Khmer Prasat Kok Po inscription (1004 CE).
